item.title: Demonstration of a Qubit Control Scheme Compatible with Superconducting Digital Signals
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Bipolar high-speed pulse sequences generated from low-frequency guiding waveforms on a single 25 GSa/s common clock achieve 40 ns single-qubit average gate fidelity of 99.94% and 120 ns CZ gate fidelity of (99.63 ± 0.02)%.

Grade 0.439 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Chenyin Sun, Yu Xu, Zihua Chen, Dayu Li, Tianzuo Sun, Chen Zha, Yuan Li, Jin Lin, Lei Jiang, Tao Rong, Tao Jiang, Shaoyu Zhan, Xueshen Wang, Shijian Wang, Wenhui Cao, Yeru Wang, Xiaomin Wang, Ming Gong, Yulin Wu, Yuhuai Li, Gang Wu, Hui Deng, Kai Yan, Sirui Cao, Futian Liang, Fusheng Chen, Qingling Zhu, Yangsen Ye, Hao Rong, Shaojun Guo, Haoran Qian, Haibin Zhang, Yisen Hu, Shaowei Li, Jinjin Li, Cheng-Zhi Peng, Xiaobo Zhu, Jian-Wei Pan

Figure

CZ gate calibration and performance: panels show coupler parameter calibrations versus threshold and guiding frequency, plus cycle-dependent cross-entropy benchmarking fidelity decay.

Asks

Can superconducting qubit single- and two-qubit gates be driven with high fidelity using common-clock digital pulse sequences without per-qubit analog microwave trigger sources?

But

Demonstrated using room-temperature AWG emulation rather than integrated cryogenic SFQ circuits; CZ fidelity standard error omits single-qubit reference error uncertainty.

Tools

guiding-waveform pulse encoding · arbitrary waveform generator at 25 GSa/s · cross-entropy benchmarking · tunable coupler transmon architecture

Abstract

Superconducting quantum computing faces a critical scalability bottleneck arising from the escalating complexity of traditional analog control infrastructure. Single-Flux-Quantum(SFQ) systems operate at cryogenic temperatures and offer a potential route to addressing these challenges. Using microwave signals at qubit-dependent frequencies to trigger SFQ pulses requires many independent analog microwave sources, limiting the potential to reduce control wiring and increase integration density. A scalable SFQ control system therefore needs a scheme that can address qubits with different transition frequencies using a common clock. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a control scheme for implementing both single- and two-qubit gates. The scheme uses guiding waveforms to rapidly generate bipolar high-speed pulse sequences on a common clock, providing a basis for future implementation in SFQ control systems. Numerically, this scheme achieves a simulated fidelity of 99.99% for 40ns R(φ, fracπ2) gates with arbitrary initial phases and 99.9% for 100ns controlled-Z(CZ) gates. Experimentally, by utilizing an arbitrary waveform generator(AWG) operated at a fixed sampling rate of 25GSa/s to deliver the bipolar high-speed pulse sequences, we successfully demonstrate 40ns single-qubit gates with an average gate fidelity of 99.94% estimated using cross-entropy benchmarking(XEB) and 120ns CZ gates with 99.63% fidelity. These results demonstrate the feasibility of common-clock encoded pulse control for both single- and two-qubit gates.

item.title: Transient Synchronization and Entanglement through Shared Dissipation in Circuit QED
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Two superconducting resonators coupled via DC-biased SQUIDs to a common auxiliary mode of loss κb exhibit an exceptional point at ξEP=|δ|/(1+|δ|), transient synchronization, and transient entanglement within ∼0.3 μs for private decay rate γd/2π=0.5 MHz.

Grade 0.435 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Areeda Ayoub, Eric R. Bittner

Figure

Logarithmic negativity EN plotted against dimensionless time τ for different cross-decay parameters ξ and thermal occupations n, showing transient entanglement generated from initial local squeezing via collective dissipation.

Asks

Can static flux-tunable SQUID couplings to a single lossy auxiliary resonator realize an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement via engineered shared dissipation in circuit QED?

But

Small-phase linear regime of SQUIDs, rotating-wave approximation, Markovian limit κb/2≫max⁡{g12+g22,γd,1/2,γd,2/2,|Δ1|,|Δ2|}, and simulation rather than experimental measurement.

Tools

adiabatic elimination · quantum Langevin equations · SQUID-based parametric coupling · logarithmic negativity

Abstract

We propose a superconducting circuit in which two resonators couple through DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode. Adiabatic elimination yields collective damping and correlated noise with an overlap ξ whose magnitude is tuned by the flux biases and whose sign follows the relative sign of the couplings. The full three-mode dynamics confirm this reduced description. For detuned resonators, we derive the exceptional-point condition, above which the mean amplitudes lock to a common frequency. For resonant modes, unequal collective decay produces transient synchronization, antiphase or in phase depending on the relative sign of the couplings, with an analytical synchronization time set by the collective decay splitting and the initial mean amplitudes. For initially separable squeezed states, the same relaxation converts local squeezing into transient entanglement, quantified by logarithmic negativity. We obtain closed-form expressions for the squeezing threshold above which entanglement appears and for the time at which it disappears. Thermal noise suppresses entanglement without changing the mean-amplitude synchronization time at fixed parameters. For realistic circuit parameters, these effects occur within a few hundred nanoseconds and are accessible through output-field measurements. A single tunable shared channel thus produces an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement, and provides a controllable source of correlated noise for superconducting circuits.

item.title: Microwave-optical quantum transduction with quantum-well exciton polaritons
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Electro-optic quantum transducer using stepped GaAs/AlGaAs quantum-well exciton polaritons achieves predicted transduction efficiency over 60% with under 0.01 added noise quanta across a ∼60 MHz bandwidth at pump power below 10 µW.

Grade 0.424 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Nicholas S. Yama, Mohammad Khalifa, Yuxuan Wei, Adbhut Gupta, Loren N. Pfeiffer, Feng Wang, Alp Sipahigil

Figure

Pump power Pc, peak transduction efficiency η, and added noise nadd as functions of cavity detuning and polariton composition, showing efficiency >60% and added noise <0.01 at microwatt pump powers.

Asks

Can quantum-well excitons be engineered via the quantum-confined Stark effect to yield high-efficiency, high-bandwidth, low-noise microwave-to-optical quantum transduction under low pump power?

Before

Vacuum electro-optic coupling is up to five orders of magnitude larger, and pump power is reduced ∼6400-fold compared to thin-film lithium niobate devices with equivalent loaded quality factors.

But

Theoretical design with numerical simulation; assumes low-density bosonic exciton regime; subject to failure modes if discrete exciton states fall within a 4ωb frequency band around the idler line.

Tools

quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) · stepped GaAs/AlGaAs quantum wells · exciton-polaritons in integrated photonic cavities · superconducting microwave LC resonators · numerical disorder modeling

Abstract

Linking superconducting quantum processors over optical fiber requires microwave-optical quantum transducers that are efficient, high-bandwidth, and low-noise. This combination has been out of reach because of the weak nonlinearities of conventional electro-optic (EO) materials. We propose a transducer with an engineered, strong EO nonlinearity using the quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) of quantum-well excitons. The QCSE transducer leverages the strong light-matter interactions and extreme polarizability of quantum well excitons. Strong coupling to an optical cavity forms exciton-polaritons whose vacuum EO coupling is up to five orders of magnitude larger than in a typical thin-film lithium niobate device. We describe a GaAs/AlGaAs stepped-quantum-well transducer design with predicted transduction efficiencies above 60% and fewer than 0.01 added noise quanta over a ∼60 MHz bandwidth, using pump powers below 10 μW and loaded optical and microwave quality factors of only 3×10⁴ and 10³. We further show that the cavity protection of the polariton provides robustness against inhomogeneous broadening of the quantum well excitons.

item.title: Logical error prediction and geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased circuit-level noise
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Response coefficients derived strictly from an unbiased reference circuit predict finite-bias circuit-level logical error rates with a median fold error of 1.09, cutting physical qubit counts by up to 42.4% (standard depolarizing) and 26.2% (superconducting-inspired) relative to square codes at physical error rate p=0.004 and target logical error rate PL,target=10−3.

Grade 0.423 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Youshin Chung, Yujin Kang, Jun Heo

Figure

Physical qubit count as a function of idle noise bias for validated rectangular surface codes versus unrotated square code baselines at p=0.004 and PL,target=10−3.

Asks

Can the logical error response to a localized circuit-level bias be inferred from an unbiased reference circuit and transferred to finite-bias conditions without geometry- or bias-specific response fitting?

Before

Neglecting bias response gives a median fold error of 1.28, while mapping the full idle-channel change directly into the baseline parameter yields 3.18.

But

Unrotated rectangular surface codes only; evaluated at bias ratios η∈{1,2,3}, 0.003≤p≤0.008, and for memory experiments run over r=max⁡(L1,L2) rounds.

Tools

Stim and PyMatching · Score-function logical sensitivity estimation · Ordinary least-squares regression · Sinter Monte Carlo sampling

Abstract

Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. Geometries selected by the model are validated through direct biased circuit-level simulations. At a physical error rate of 0.004 and a target logical error rate of 10^{-3}, the validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models, respectively, relative to unrotated square codes. These results provide a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design.

item.title: Simplifying models of noisy stabilizer QEC on leakage qubits by Pauli twirling
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Noisy stabilizer QEC cycles with leakage map to classical Markov processes over joint syndrome and leakage configurations, with logical Pauli channels associated to each transition. Yields exact transfer-matrix formulas for logical success probability across repeated cycles.

Grade 0.423 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Alex Kwiatkowski, Aaron J. Friedman

Asks

How to model multi-cycle logical performance and logical error rates in stabilizer QEC when physical qubits suffer leakage.

Before

Stabilizer QEC cycle with Pauli-stochastic noise maps to classical Markov process over syndrome states alone, without leakage.

But

Applies after leakage-dephased Pauli twirling. Assumes stabilizer QEC architecture.

Tools

leakage-dephased Pauli twirling · classical Markov process over joint syndrome-leakage patterns · transfer-matrix method

Abstract

The growing capabilities of quantum error-correction (QEC) experiments make it increasingly important to develop methods that predict or assess logical performance over many QEC cycles. Prior work has shown that a stabilizer QEC cycle subject to Pauli-stochastic noise can be modeled by a classical Markov process over syndrome states, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each syndrome transition. Here, we extend this framework to systems in which physical qubits are subject to leakage. We first develop the theory of leakage-dephased Pauli twirling and show that twirled processes can be expressed in terms of Pauli maps on the computational subspace, conditioned on transitions between leakage patterns. We apply this theory to noisy stabilizer QEC with leakage, demonstrating that a QEC cycle with leakage can be modeled by a classical Markov process over the joint syndrome and leakage patterns, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each joint transition. Finally, we derive a transfer-matrix description of repeated QEC cycles and an exact transfer-matrix expression for the success probability of a QEC memory experiment. This framework connects leaky error models of the individual components of the QEC cycle to many-cycle logical performance and provides a foundation for logical characterization and benchmarking methods that can account for leakage.

item.title: Dynamical Decoupling via Continuous Unitary Design
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Continuous-unitary-design-inspired dynamical decoupling (CUDD) eliminates first-order static noise during finite-duration pulses by concatenating continuous unitary design trajectories, outperforming CPMG, XY4, and UR4 against Rabi-amplitude errors and detuning.

Grade 0.413 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Xiaodong Yang, Jun Li

Figure

Coherence protection efficiency η plotted against injected Rabi errors and detuning offsets on superconducting qubit Q4 at pulse interval τ=60 ns. CUDD maintains higher protection efficiency over wider error ranges than CPMG, XY4, and UR4 sequences.

Asks

Can dynamical decoupling achieve universal decoupling and control-error robustness under realistic finite-duration pulses without assuming instantaneous bang-bang control?

But

Demonstrated on single qubits with 1 ns waveform resolution; assumes static noise during continuous segments and piecewise-constant control parameters.

Tools

Continuous unitary designs · Average Hamiltonian theory · 17-qubit superconducting processor (QZ01-surface_code) · Pulse-level microwave and flux control

Abstract

Dynamical decoupling is a cornerstone of quantum control for protecting and engineering quantum systems. However, conventional schemes rely on idealized instantaneous pulses, limiting their performance under realistic finite-duration and imperfect controls. To overcome this limitation, we establish a dynamical decoupling framework based on continuous unitary designs, which intrinsically suppresses arbitrary static noise during continuous control. We further derive closed-form phase conditions to suppress Rabi-amplitude errors, unifying universal decoupling, finite-pulse compatibility, and control-error robustness within a single analytical framework. We experimentally validate our approach on a superconducting quantum cloud platform, demonstrating significantly extended coherence times and the highest robustness against Rabi-amplitude errors and detuning among the tested sequences.

item.title: Multilevel Effects and the Limits of the Quantum Rabi Model in Ultrastrong Coupling system
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Diagonal energy corrections via Löwdin partitioning substantially suppress spectral errors caused by two-level truncation in ultrastrong coupling, but refitting constant Rabi model parameters leaves systematic deviations for actual circuit parameters.

Grade 0.410 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Akiyoshi Tomonaga

Figure

Transition frequencies plotted against normalized external magnetic flux f. The full circuit spectrum is compared to the two-level truncated model, diagonal Löwdin corrections, and rediagonalized second-order effective models.

Asks

To what extent do truncated higher atomic levels alter low-energy spectra in ultrastrongly coupled multilevel circuits, and where do two-level or perturbative Rabi models remain quantitatively accurate?

But

Restricted to second-order perturbative treatment of higher atomic levels; full rediagonalization with off-diagonal terms fails to improve accuracy when state mixing becomes non-perturbative.

Tools

capacitively shunted flux qubit · Löwdin partitioning · circuit Hamiltonian · vector network analyzer

Abstract

The spectrum of artificial atoms coupled to resonators in the ultrastrong coupling regime have been analyzed using the quantum Rabi model over a wide range of coupling strengths. However, the accuracy of models obtained by truncating multilevel artificial atoms to two levels, as well as the correspondence between effective parameters extracted from spectral fitting and the bare parameters of the circuit Hamiltonian, depends on the multilevel structure of the system. In this study, I analyze the spectrum of an ultrastrongly coupled circuit consisting of a multilevel superconducting artificial atom and a resonator using a circuit Hamiltonian, and investigate the effects of truncating higher atomic levels on the low-energy spectrum. Based on Löwdin partitioning, I evaluate the contributions of virtual transitions through higher atomic levels and show that diagonal energy corrections reduce the errors arising from simple two-level truncation over a wide parameter range. I also show that there are parameter regimes in which readjustment of the effective Rabi parameters successfully reproduces the multilevel spectrum, while systematic deviations remain in other regimes. These results demonstrate the necessity of separately evaluating two-level truncation, perturbative corrections, and effective-parameter fitting in ultrastrongly coupled systems, and provide guidance for quantitative spectral analysis of multilevel quantum circuits.

item.title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Demonstrated fault-tolerant lattice-surgery teleportation between two distance-three surface-code logical qubits on a 41-transmon chip. Circuit depletion improved logical success probabilities from 0.57 to 0.65 for Z basis states and from 0.66 to 0.73 for X basis states.

Grade 0.401 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Luca Hofele, Yongxin Song, Áron Márton, Ian Hesner, Ilya Besedin, Jakob Ekert, Jonathan Trebst, Franccois Swiadek, Felix Henrich, Dante Colao Zanúz, Mohsen Bahrami Panah, Lukas Bödeker, Nicholas Gialouris, Chrysander D. Hagen, Marek Pechal, Jean Claude Besse, Markus Müller, Christoph Hellings, Andreas Wallraff

Figure

Error-corrected logical expectation values across three teleportation circuits (fully modular, partially depleted, and fully depleted) for four logical eigenstates. Depleting non-essential stabilizer rounds increases teleported output fidelity.

Asks

How do logical observables evolve throughout fault-tolerant lattice surgery, and can circuit depletion optimize logical teleportation performance?

Before

Fully modular logical teleportation circuit achieved logical expectation values of |obreak⟨mSmZZˆL2⟩|=0.14 and |⟨mXXˆL2⟩|=0.32.

But

Demonstrated for Pauli eigenstates only; full quantum state tomography not implemented. Physical error rates remain above fault-tolerance threshold.

Tools

41 frequency-tunable transmon superconducting circuit · distance-three rotated planar surface code · flux-activated CZ gates · multiplexed dispersive readout with Purcell filters · lattice surgery

Abstract

Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.
